paragraph_changes.before: A gateway that screens uniform resource locators (URLs) must detect phishing without burdening legitimate users with false warnings or delay. This Praxis examines that problem through CyberSentinel, a system that combines structural classification, selective expert execution and distribution monitoring. Structural features increase internal recall by 64.07 percentage points over length alone at a 0.7747% false-positive rate. That advantage does not extend to external specificity. Follow-up experiments show that scheme spelling changes the structural model's decisions. A separate scheme-neutral refit and recalibration remove this sensitivity across 8,622 pairs, although both false positives and true-positive detections decline. Paired errors explain why changing the gate offers limited improvement, and exploratory routing gains do not transfer externally. Monitoring detects a change in inputs, but its escalation policy adds false alerts without improving gold recall. A larger comparison, with 1,392 positive domains and every system at the recall ceiling, supports the two-point recall-only noninferiority margin for both cascades against the transformer, conditional on independent labeled pairs. Distinct domains do not establish that independence. Direct measurements also show that sparse expert calls increase scoring time and the tail of the scoring-time distribution. Separately, worker-owned clients reduce median paired 95th-percentile latency by 79.68% on synthetic structural-only Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) requests. Comparable predictions agree, while admission order changes. The original hypotheses and combined follow-up requirements remain unsupported. The contribution is an empirical basis for redesign: useful internal structural information, a verified scheme-invariance property, limits on expert correction and a measured opportunity to reduce service cost.
paragraph_changes.after: High internal accuracy does not establish reliable phishing detection across sources. This Praxis evaluates CyberSentinel, a uniform resource locator (URL) gateway combining structural classification, a character transformer and distribution monitoring. Paired interventions test representation, routing and execution cost. Internal feature gains fail to transfer: both models falsely flag 2,261 of 2,497 certified external negatives, imposing a 90.5487% floor on routing between unchanged decisions. Wider gates add errors without repairs. Scheme interventions expose input dependence. A refit achieves invariance but loses detections and retains poor specificity. In shuffled-label controls, small random coefficients rank structured validation labels despite probabilities near 0.5; component removal, 99 permutations and stricter convergence support this explanation. Separately, worker-owned clients reduce median paired 95th-percentile latency by 79.68% in synthetic structural-only Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) measurements, with a similar no-model improvement. Actual expert calls increase computation on another workload. The operating hypotheses remain unsupported. This controlled failure analysis identifies what redesign requires: transferable discrimination, useful expert corrections, representation stability with detection quality, and measured request-path efficiency.

paragraph_changes.before: Patterns learned from one URL collection may be unreliable in another. Even an internal test can overstate generalization when related domains occur in both training and evaluation data. Separating domains makes that test more demanding. A second model introduces a different issue: its additional capacity matters only if it corrects enough first-stage errors to justify its cost. These concerns motivate the study's evaluation of domain separation, selective execution and monitoring under shared detection and service requirements.
paragraph_changes.after: A model can learn a useful association within one collection without learning a dependable signal for another. Separating domains removes overlap, but shared collection conventions can remain. Routing to an expert helps only when the second model corrects the first. The study therefore examines both transfer across sources and whether changes to representation, routing or monitoring address the observed errors.

paragraph_changes.before: An inline phishing gateway must satisfy several demands at once. It must detect threats, keep the false-positive rate (FPR) low on external sources and respond within an acceptable time. An expensive expert model must contribute corrections that justify calling it. Latency and request errors must also be measured through the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) path used by callers. The problem addressed here is whether these benefits can be obtained together. Meeting an isolated detection or timing target would leave the gateway's overall suitability unresolved.
paragraph_changes.after: An inline phishing gateway must detect threats while limiting false warnings and delay. These demands interact: an expert call consumes resources, and a recall gain may be unusable if it sharply increases false positives. The research problem is to establish whether a low-cost structural detector, selective character-model execution and distribution monitoring can satisfy the detection and service constraints together. Success on one metric alone cannot establish gateway suitability.

paragraph_changes.before: Poor transfer does not, by itself, tell an engineer what to change. The model may depend on unsuitable input cues, its operating point may no longer fit the source, or its expert may be unable to correct the cases sent to it. Delays may arise independently in request processing. CyberSentinel examines these possibilities through separate comparisons so that each proposed change can be judged against the behavior it is intended to improve. Chapter 3 describes the limits of the publisher labels and the evaluation information already available to the analyst.
paragraph_changes.after: Poor external performance has several possible explanations. A detector may rely on collection-specific cues, its threshold may transfer poorly, or the expert may share the errors it is expected to repair. Request handling can add delay independently of those detection failures. Paired decisions and controlled interventions test these explanations; Chapter 3 defines the populations and the limitations of their labels.

The resulting evidence provides a basis for choosing the next intervention and judging whether it succeeds.
paragraph_changes.after: Reliable cascaded detection requires discrimination that transfers across sources, disagreements that let one model correct another, and measured execution costs. The experiments identify where CyberSentinel falls short and how its behavior changes under specific interventions. The resulting failure analysis establishes constraints that a redesign must address.

This provides a URL-gateway example of the downstream-error problem analyzed by Jitkrittum et al. (2023): greater model capacity and preserved recall alone do not establish expert value (Sections 4.8.1 and 4.10.2).

paragraph_changes.before: Good ranking does not ensure useful decisions at the threshold a gateway actually uses. Receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC) summarizes ranking across thresholds, while precision–recall analysis is particularly informative with imbalanced classes (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015). Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) draws on all four confusion categories (Chicco & Jurman, 2020), and proper scoring rules assess probabilities (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007). These measures help explain performance. Counts at the locked threshold remain essential because the operating budgets apply to those decisions.
paragraph_changes.after: Ranking, probability quality and operating-point error answer different questions. Receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC) measures pairwise ordering across thresholds; even narrowly separated scores can have high AUC. Precision–recall analysis is informative under class imbalance (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015), Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) uses all four confusion categories (Chicco & Jurman, 2020), and proper scoring rules assess probabilities (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007). None substitutes for the false-positive and detection counts at the threshold a gateway will use. This distinction also matters when interpreting shuffled-label controls.

paragraph_changes.before: An expert helps only where it is better than the model it replaces. Jitkrittum et al. (2023, Section 3.2) formalize this through a cost-sensitive rule based on the difference between the models' conditional probabilities of being correct. First-stage confidence alone may not reveal that difference, especially with specialization, label noise or distribution shift. Ovadia et al. (2019) also show that uncertainty estimates can deteriorate as distributions change. CyberSentinel therefore counts both the errors repaired and those introduced by selected calls at frozen thresholds. Separate computation and HTTP measurements establish the cost. This evaluates the selected calls without claiming to implement an optimal deferral rule.
paragraph_changes.after: Expert selection is a comparison of errors on the same input. Jitkrittum et al. (2023, Section 3.2) formalize a cost-sensitive decision using the difference between the models' conditional probabilities of correctness. Uncertainty in the first model need not identify an advantage for the second, particularly under specialization, label noise or distribution shift. Ovadia et al. (2019) show that uncertainty estimates themselves can deteriorate under shift. The present study consequently measures available corrections, selected repairs and introduced errors at fixed thresholds, then measures expert cost separately. It evaluates this gateway's calls without claiming an optimal deferral rule.

paragraph_changes.before: An aggregate performance score may reveal poor transfer without explaining how to improve the detector. This study addresses that gap by testing specific changes in a URL gateway. It measures sensitivity to scheme spelling, verifies its removal through a separate refit, examines the corrections available from expert selection and evaluates a change in client processing. Monitoring is assessed through the decisions that follow its alerts. Table 2.1 relates these experiments to earlier work on robustness, adaptation and deferral.
paragraph_changes.after: Poor transfer is an observation; it does not by itself identify a useful engineering change. Aggregate accuracy cannot reveal whether a detector depends on formatting, whether an expert can correct its errors, or whether delay arises outside inference. The study addresses this gap by connecting each explanation to a controlled comparison. Table 2.1 places that contribution alongside research on robustness, adaptation and deferral.

paragraph_changes.before: The comparisons follow the decisions an engineer faces after an unsuccessful evaluation. Scheme interventions then test the representation, paired errors bound the corrections available from an expert, and shuffled labels probe validation ranking. Separate scoring and HTTP measurements identify where costs arise. Together, these comparisons provide an evaluated basis for redesign.

If both models make the same false-positive decision, routing between them at those thresholds cannot correct it. The original external cohort demonstrates that limit. Representation changes similarly need labeled specificity checks after invariance is verified, and alert-driven policies need evidence of useful corrections. paragraph_changes.after: Before widening a gate, count available repairs, selected repairs and introduced errors on labeled data from the intended source. After changing representation or acting on a monitoring alert, test specificity as well as the intended benefit. Tranco supplies a popularity-based control with a different evidential role from certified labels (Le Pochat et al., 2019).

paragraph_changes.before: The client result is useful where the application's response requirements permit it. All 99,999 comparable primary pairs preserve prediction fields, while admission order changes and the timeout pair remains noncomparable. An application requiring identical order would need further work. Expert counters and p99 also deserve attention because p95 can obscure rare-call costs. These observations justify examining client ownership on this path; other hardware, arrival processes and workloads require their own evaluations.
paragraph_changes.after: Service evaluation should measure the complete request path against an explicit response contract. Here, 99,999 comparable predictions agree even though admission order changes and one pair times out. Expert counters and p99 reveal costs that a low call fraction can obscure. Different hardware, arrival processes and workloads require separate measurements.

paragraph_changes.before: Domain separation cannot remove a shared collection mechanism. PhiUSIIL lacks independent per-row provenance for a noncircular source-only classifier, and a scheme intervention cannot explain every source of poor transfer. The new shuffled-label records verify consumed inputs, but their rankings vary and true validation labels select their thresholds. Only five permutations are available. They cannot support a formal significance test, establish the absence of leakage or authenticate historical fits.
paragraph_changes.after: Domain separation does not remove shared collection conventions. PhiUSIIL lacks independent per-row provenance for a noncircular source-only classifier. The control analyses establish a reproducible contribution from the HTTPS term and broad ranking variation under randomized training labels on fixed partitions. They do not identify how that convention arose or each feature's contribution. Term removal retains correlated predictors, and the 99 permutations describe algorithmic sensitivity rather than independent populations. True validation labels select the five controls' thresholds; historical fits still lack consumed-input authentication.

paragraph_changes.before: The next detection study should concentrate on errors shared by the models. New information or different operating points may create corrections that the present gate cannot select. Those changes should be assessed on independently adjudicated, time-indexed sources. Service work should cross workload with session order and examine open-loop arrivals. It should also evaluate stable admission order separately from request-correlated prediction equality. These proposals extend the present evidence without changing its thresholds or decisions.
paragraph_changes.after: Detection redesign requires independently adjudicated, time-indexed source data whose formatting conventions are recorded independently of outcome. Those sources should support evaluation of expert repairs, harms and cost. Service studies should balance workload and session order, test open-loop arrivals, and distinguish stable admission order from prediction equality.

paragraph_changes.before: This Praxis gives engineers evidence for redesigning a URL gateway. Structural information provides substantial internal value beyond length alone. The scheme experiments identify a sensitivity and verify its removal through a separate refit and recalibration, while measuring losses in true-positive detections and reductions in false positives. Paired predictions identify the expert's available corrections; routing records show whether they are selected. These findings clarify which errors remain and which interventions could change them.
paragraph_changes.after: This Praxis provides a connected failure analysis of a URL-only phishing gateway. Internal feature gains do not establish external specificity. Interventions with the model held fixed identify scheme dependence, while a refit removes that dependence without delivering reliable detection. Audited randomized controls explain how small fitted coefficients can produce substantial AUC when validation labels retain structure.

paragraph_changes.before: Both cascades meet the two-point recall-only noninferiority margin on 1,392 positive domains, conditional on independent labeled pairs. Separately, worker-owned clients reduce median paired p95 by 79.68% on synthetic structural-only HTTP requests. Comparable predictions agree, while admission order changes. Sparse expert calls increase summed scoring time and scoring p99 in the computation experiment. That cost cannot be pooled with the HTTP result. Retained inputs, outcomes and schedules support further examination.
paragraph_changes.after: Errors shared by the models and introduced by selected calls explain why routing fails to help. Preserving recall when every positive is already detected adds little practical evidence. Sparse expert calls increase scoring work. In the separate synthetic structural-only setup, worker-owned clients reduce median paired HTTP p95 by 79.68%, preserving comparable predictions while changing admission order.

paragraph_changes.before: CyberSentinel does not meet H1–H3 and is not qualified for deployment. The findings give its redesign a measured starting point: improve discrimination where model errors coincide, select expert calls that offer useful corrections and examine client ownership to reduce request-path cost.
paragraph_changes.after: CyberSentinel does not meet H1–H3, but its evaluation gives reproducible reasons for redesign. Where errors coincide, the available evidence must change. inserted_paragraphs.text: P tests three explanations for the ranking spread: an input or scoring error, incomplete numerical optimization, and a small random fitted direction aligned with structured validation labels. The audit checks partition hashes, domain/identity/canonical separation, actual consumed label permutations, training-only scaling and saved-score reconstruction, then independently recalculates tie-aware AUC. Subtracting the explicit is_https logit contribution from each frozen model measures sensitivity to that term without refitting or changing another coefficient. It is not a causal importance estimate because correlated scheme information can remain in other predictors.

A frozen conditional randomization protocol then schedules 99 additional training-label permutations, PCG64 seeds 1000–1098. It keeps the 166,248 training rows, 32,695 validation rows, training-fitted scaler, estimator settings and solver seed fixed. Every attempt is retained, including warnings or failures, with no seed substitutions or outcome-driven extension. True validation labels remain fixed and no threshold is selected. A reference comparison independently permutes validation labels using seed 210000 plus the fit seed. Constant-score AUC, removal of the HTTPS term and inverse-domain-size weighting provide further checks. Empirical quantiles summarize this fixed-data algorithmic distribution; they are not confidence intervals for new populations or a test certifying the absence of leakage (Ojala & Garriga, 2010).

A separate frozen convergence check continues each of the five saved fits from its coefficients and intercept, preserving the permuted labels and objective. Only tolerance and the iteration budget change: tol=1e-7 and max_iter=20000, with warm_start=True. Each seed is attempted once. The diagnostic reports AUC changes and first-order optimality residuals for the sum of class-weighted logistic losses and an L1 penalty weighted by 1/C, with an unpenalized intercept. Dividing residuals by total sample weight puts them on a mean-loss scale. This tests sensitivity to the original stopping tolerance; it does not replace the original results.

The saved coefficients and fixed-score intervention directly support that explanation. Seeds 43 and 46 assign is_https coefficients of −0.008797 and −0.009530; their AUCs are 0.6419 and 0.6965. Removing only that term lowers their AUCs to 0.4031 and 0.4195. Seed 45 assigns a positive coefficient of 0.004024: its AUC rises from 0.3940 to 0.4934 when the term is removed. The same operation changes seed 42 from 0.4718 to 0.5476 and seed 44 from 0.5487 to 0.5883. These are all five original controls. The intervention identifies a substantial contribution to ranking from this term, without claiming that it uniquely accounts for the multifeature score.

All 99 scheduled additional permutations complete without warnings and below the iteration limit. Against unchanged validation labels, AUC ranges from 0.1046 to 0.9496, with mean 0.4779, median 0.4479 and empirical 2.5th–97.5th percentiles [0.2061, 0.7718]. Of the 99 fits, 12 reach or exceed the original maximum of 0.6965. This frequency describes the scheduled randomizations; it is not a leakage p-value. The complete larger set reproduces the broad spread, showing that the original high value need not result from choosing a favorable seed after fitting.

Two reference comparisons locate the spread. With each fitted score held fixed and validation labels independently shuffled, mean AUC is 0.5000 and the full range is [0.4933, 0.5066]. Constant scores give AUC 0.5. Across training permutations, the descriptive Spearman correlation between the HTTPS coefficient and true-label AUC is -0.8253. Removing the explicit term changes mean absolute departure from 0.5 from 0.1424 to 0.0851. Equal total weight per validation domain still gives AUCs spanning 0.0770–0.9554; repeated URLs within domains are therefore insufficient to explain the spread. These calculations retain one fixed collection and do not establish independent campaign sampling.

Stricter optimization leaves the ranking explanation intact. All five continuations finish without warnings, and the largest absolute AUC change is 0.000406. The maximum first-order residual, scaled to mean loss, is 3.48e-09. The highest original control changes from 0.696523 to 0.696632. Alongside verification of the consumed inputs and independent score reconstruction, these results show that the original stopping tolerance cannot adequately explain the observed AUC spread.

The controls support a computational explanation for the ranking: small random fitted coefficients act on validation data that retain class-related structure, producing substantial ranking without confident probabilities. Component removal, repeated randomization and convergence checks test different parts of this explanation. Correlated features also contribute, and the causal role of collection source remains unidentified. The diagnosis does not certify that all leakage is absent, authenticate historical fits, or validate threshold-selected performance.

The shuffled-label diagnosis adds a methodological contribution to the failure analysis. Scores can be nearly constant yet retain an informative ordering when small residual coefficients act on validation data with a strong association between format and class. Each check examines a different part of that explanation: the audit verifies what reached fitting, term removal exposes one contribution to ranking, the larger randomization set reproduces the variation, and stricter optimization preserves it. Assessing a control therefore requires its randomization design, fitted state and score ordering as well as its score mean.

The control-mechanism analysis uses only the original training and validation partitions. Its protocol retains five saved P models, a fixed set of 99 additional label permutations and five stricter numerical continuations. The public dissertation/2026-10-15 directory contains protocols, source, aggregate coefficients and metrics, a diagnostic report and independent metric-verification results. Reproduction instructions distinguish aggregate recalculation from runs requiring original partitions and restricted fit receipts. Cache matrices, URLs, domains and record identifiers remain excluded. The hypothesis criteria and decisions are unchanged; the retained protocols document the diagnostic analyses separately from the original hypothesis tests.
